headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: gpt-researcher’s broad egress plus xonsh’s writable shell/filesystem create a dangerous default pair.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: gpt-researcher ingests web/research content and can call MCP, while xonsh executes shell commands and reads files. If gpt-researcher outputs untrusted text that xonsh later treats as commands, prompt injection is plausible in default research workflows. The pair lacks a documented provenance barrier, so uncertainty is escalated.
conditions: IF gpt-researcher output is copied into xonsh commands or scripts
IF xonsh consumes research text as executable shell input
IF a shared MCP or stdin/stdout bridge is used without provenance tagging
mitigations: Use a strict copy/paste boundary and never execute generated text directly
Wrap xonsh execution in a command allowlist
Add provenance labels to all gpt-researcher outputs
Disable MCP bridging between the agents unless reviewed
requires-engineering: add parser-level escaping and command sandboxing

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents read files and have broad network egress; gpt-researcher also handles API secrets and documents, while xonsh can write filesystem contents and inspect environment variables. In a shared workspace, either agent can expose sensitive local documents or secrets through outbound requests or generated outputs. The default blast radius includes exfiltration.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same workspace or home directory
IF gpt-researcher is pointed at local documents containing secrets
IF xonsh reads environment variables or files that gpt-researcher can access
mitigations: Separate workspaces and mount only least-privilege directories
Move API keys out of shared environment variables
Block outbound network for xonsh unless needed
Review gpt-researcher inputs before file ingestion
requires-engineering: add DLP or egress proxy controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: gpt-researcher can spawn subprocesses and read files, and xonsh can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write the filesystem. Both can mutate the same local state, so concurrent runs can overwrite files, race on artifacts, or corrupt outputs. xonsh’s lack of multiple-instance support increases the conflict risk.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or notebook tree
IF gpt-researcher writes reports while xonsh edits files in place
IF two xonsh instances or one xonsh plus gpt-researcher run concurrently
mitigations: Assign separate output directories per agent
Serialize writes with a lock file
Run xonsh in a single-instance workflow
Use git or filesystem snapshots before edits
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-researcher produces research reports and citations, and xonsh can act on shell commands or notebook workflows. If xonsh treats gpt-researcher output as authoritative, errors or hallucinated citations can cascade into incorrect commands, file edits, or notebook actions. Verification is not documented, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF xonsh consumes gpt-researcher reports without human review
IF generated citations or facts are used to build shell commands
IF downstream actions are taken from research output
mitigations: Require human review before execution
Compare claims against source URLs before acting
Keep research output read-only until validated
Use a checklist for command generation from reports
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking gates

E_compliance.rationale: gpt-researcher explicitly handles research queries, local documents, citations, and multiple API keys, while xonsh touches filesystem contents, configuration, and environment variables. If regulated or sensitive data is placed in the shared workflow, the pair can create retention and residency mismatches through outbound APIs and shell access. The profiles do not document matching compliance controls.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through gpt-researcher or xonsh
IF API-backed research sends sensitive content to third-party services
IF retention or deletion requirements apply to shared files or notebooks
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair’s workspace
Restrict gpt-researcher to non-sensitive sources
Document retention and deletion rules for outputs
Separate secrets from research inputs
requires-engineering: perform a compliance review for each data class
